content: Photosensitivity refers to the degree to which an object reacts when exposed to photons of light. In the context of medicine, individuals who are photosensitive may experience discomfort or develop sunburns easily when exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light. This UV light can originate from natural sunlight or artificial sources such as tanning beds. Photosensitivity in humans is often caused by an allergic reaction or as a side effect of certain medications. In electronic engineering, specific devices like photodiodes and charge-coupled devices (CCDs) are intentionally designed to be sensitive to light. These devices utilize the photoelectric effect, which involves the emission of electrons from a material when it absorbs electromagnetic radiation. When light, a form of electromagnetic radiation, strikes the active surface of these devices, the electrical current flowing through them or the electrical charge stored within them changes in proportion to the intensity and wavelength of the light. This property enables these devices to perform various sensing and regulatory functions. For instance, a photoresistor circuit can detect ambient light levels to automatically turn on a street lamp at dusk. Similarly, digital cameras employ CCDs with high sensitivity to light, allowing them to convert incoming photons into precise electrical charges. These charges are then encoded into binary files, which can be stored and later displayed on a computer screen or other media. In the field of chemistry, photosensitive chemicals undergo chemical reactions when exposed to light. Examples of such chemicals include hydrogen peroxide and numerous prescription drugs. To prevent photodegradation, these substances are typically stored in tinted or opaque containers until they are needed. Photosensitive devices also include the human retina and photographic film. Photographic film is photosensitive because its material undergoes a chemical reaction when exposed to light. Common photosensitive substances include alkali salts and silver halides.
